items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.

items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.

items.title: If something grows at 3% per year, it doubles in 23 years
items.claim: Compound growth at rate r% has a fixed doubling time of about 70/r years (rule of 70) or 72/r (rule of 72). The doubling time doesn't change as the quantity grows. That's what 'exponential' means — proportional rate, not larger jumps.
items.prompt: Why is the doubling time constant?

options.text: For exponential growth dN/dt = kN, N(t) = N0 * e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k. Independent of N0 — the time to go from 1 to 2 equals the time to go from 1000 to 2000
Only applies to populations of bacteria

items.reveal:
Exponential growth: dN/dt = k * N. Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k.

Rule of 70/72: if k% per period, doubling time ≈ 70/k (or 72/k) periods. At 7%/year, doubles in ~10 years. At 1%/year, doubles in ~70 years. At 0.5%/year (current global population growth), doubles in ~140 years.

Exponential growth is unrealistic for long times — no real system maintains constant growth rate forever. The logistic model corrects: dN/dt = k * N * (1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity.

Logistic solution: N(t) = K / (1 + ((K - N_0)/N_0) * e^(-kt)). Starts exponential (when N << K), saturates at K.

Applications:
- Epidemics: early growth (susceptible >> infected) is exponential; saturates as susceptibles deplete (or interventions take effect). The famous 'flatten the curve' is intervening in this growth equation.
- Populations: many wild populations roughly logistic. Carrying capacity set by food, predation, disease.
- Innovation diffusion: technology adoption (smartphones, electric cars) often logistic.
- Tumour growth: early stages can be exponential; later stages limited by blood supply.

Misinterpretations:
- 'Exponential' is loosely used to mean 'fast growth'. Mathematically, it means proportional growth. A linear quantity can grow faster than an exponential one in the short term.
- Confusing exponential growth (rate proportional to value) with super-exponential (faster than any fixed exponential).
- Underestimating doubling times. Many people fail the 'penny doubling' problem: a penny doubled daily for 30 days becomes ~10 million dollars.
items.why: Exponential growth feels like 'fast growth'. Mathematically it's something specific: constant percentage rate, constant doubling time. Understanding doubling times is key to understanding epidemics, populations, finance, and Moore's law.
